title: Ancient Glue May Have Helped Neanderthals Fight Germs
summary:
Neanderthals were ancient humans who lived long ago. They made a sticky glue called birch tar by heating the bark of birch trees. They used it to stick stone points onto wooden handles to make tools.

Now scientists think birch tar may also have been used as medicine.

Researchers from universities in Germany, England, Belgium and Canada made their own birch tar. They used old methods, like heating bark in a sealed pit in the ground, or burning bark next to a stone.

Then they tested the tar on germs. Every sample slowed the growth of a type of bacteria that often infects wounds. Some of these germs are hard to stop with modern medicine.

There are other clues, too. People around the world have used birch tar as medicine, and Neanderthals used plants and cared for each other. The team leader, Tjaark Siemssen, said there is growing evidence of medicine use among Neanderthals.
why_it_matters: It shows that people long ago may have found clever ways to care for cuts, just like we use bandages today.
